claims.claim: A reader of The Inheritance finds Hobb epic and Lindholm more to the point.
claims.quote: Lindholm writes more to the point

claims.claim: Readers report the books are lived rather than read.
claims.quote: you don't so much read them as live them

claims.claim: Every chapter of Assassin's Apprentice opens with a long epigraph excerpted from an in-world history of the Six Duchies.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver (Campbellsville University), 'History in the Margins: Epigraphs and Negative Space in Robin Hobb's Assassin's Apprentice', Mythlore 41.1 (Fall/Winter 2022) 45-66
claims.quote: Each chapter of the novel begins with a lengthy epigraph

claims.claim: Oliver characterises the register of those in-world history epigraphs as a formal history in a distant, scholarly voice, set against the personal first-person narrative that follows.
claims.quote: largely a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice

claims.claim: Oliver calls the chapter-opening history dry and impersonal, and says the personal main text feels more authoritative and satisfying than it does.
claims.quote: the dry, impersonal, but objective history beginning the chapter

claims.claim: The chapter-13 epigraph describing Fitz's stepmother Patience carries no sign of the writer's own relationship to her.
claims.quote: contains no hint of the author's relationship to her

claims.claim: In place of personal knowledge the Patience epigraph cites testimony from her nursemaids and publicly available information.
claims.quote: evidentiary quotes from her nursemaids and publicly available information

claims.claim: Oliver names the novel's most striking stylistic element its continual insistence on describing what is not happening.
claims.quote: continual insistence on describing what is not happening

claims.claim: The device Oliver labels 'negative narration' works through sentences that open by saying what a character is not doing or feeling.
claims.quote: sentences that start by telling what a character is not doing

claims.claim: Negative constructions are so frequent in the novel's early chapters that scarcely a page passes without obvious examples.
claims.quote: scarcely a page goes by without obvious examples

claims.claim: Although the frequency of negative constructions falls off later, Oliver says the mode remains one of the book's predominant ones throughout.
claims.quote: remains one of the predominant modes throughout

claims.claim: When Fitz invents a prophetic vision to persuade a duchess, his sentences shift into extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language and parallelism.
claims.quote: extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language, and parallelism

claims.claim: Oliver reads that stylistic shift as marking Fitz's move from a discourse of history into a discourse of fantasy.
claims.quote: Fitz marks his shift from a discourse of history

claims.claim: Late in the novel the epigraphs take on the style of imaginative fiction in place of the style of scholarly discourse.
claims.quote: increasingly infected by the style of imaginative fiction

claims.claim: At the chapter-15 epigraph a poetic lyricism enters the register of the supposedly scholarly history.
claims.quote: a poetic lyricism creeps into his style in the epigraph
